lessons.name: Correction needs room: 2⁴ = 16 codewords sit sparsely inside 2⁷ = 128 possible words (16 < 128) — the redundancy is exactly what lets a flipped word be traced back to its origin.
lessons.why: Correction needs room: 2⁴ = 16 codewords sit sparsely inside 2⁷ = 128 possible words (16 < 128) — the redundancy is exactly what lets a flipped word be traced back to its origin.

lessons.name: A minimum distance of 3 corrects ⌊(d−1)/2⌋ = ⌊2/2⌋ = 1 error: any single flip lands strictly nearer its own codeword than any other.
lessons.why: A minimum distance of 3 corrects ⌊(d−1)/2⌋ = ⌊2/2⌋ = 1 error: any single flip lands strictly nearer its own codeword than any other.

lessons.name: The same distance-3 code DETECTS d − 1 = 2 errors — two flips can never reach another codeword, so they are always noticed (though not corrected).
lessons.why: The same distance-3 code DETECTS d − 1 = 2 errors — two flips can never reach another codeword, so they are always noticed (though not corrected).

lessons.name: Hamming(7,4) is a PERFECT code: each of the 16 codewords owns a sphere of 1 (itself) + 7 (single-bit flips) = 8, and 16 × 8 = 128 = 2⁷ — the spheres tile the whole 7-bit space exactly, no word wasted.
lessons.why: Hamming(7,4) is a PERFECT code: each of the 16 codewords owns a sphere of 1 (itself) + 7 (single-bit flips) = 8, and 16 × 8 = 128 = 2⁷ — the spheres tile the whole 7-bit space exactly, no word wasted.

lessons.name: Hamming(7,4): 4 data bits + 3 parity bits = 7, carrying 2⁴ = 16 codewords — three redundant bits protect four.
lessons.why: Hamming(7,4): 4 data bits + 3 parity bits = 7, carrying 2⁴ = 16 codewords — three redundant bits protect four.

lessons.name: The (3,1) repetition code corrects one flip by MAJORITY: [1,1,1] with one bit flipped still shows two 1s, and 2·2 > 3 makes two a strict majority of three.
lessons.why: The (3,1) repetition code corrects one flip by MAJORITY: [1,1,1] with one bit flipped still shows two 1s, and 2·2 > 3 makes two a strict majority of three.

lessons.name: The minimum distance d = 3 satisfies the Singleton bound d ≤ n − k + 1 = 7 − 4 + 1 = 4 — no code can beat it, and Hamming sits one below.
lessons.why: The minimum distance d = 3 satisfies the Singleton bound d ≤ n − k + 1 = 7 − 4 + 1 = 4 — no code can beat it, and Hamming sits one below.

lessons.name: A linear XOR checksum catches any single flip: XOR is self-inverse, so flipping a word by d and re-checking recovers exactly d — (a ⊕ d) ⊕ a = d, for every a. The error cannot hide.
lessons.why: A linear XOR checksum catches any single flip: XOR is self-inverse, so flipping a word by d and re-checking recovers exactly d — (a ⊕ d) ⊕ a = d, for every a. The error cannot hide.

lessons.name: THE XOR CHECKSUM IS ITS OWN UNDOING, OVER ALL 256 PAIRS. Applying a key twice returns the message — (a XOR b) XOR b = a — which is why XOR is a checksum and a cipher at once, and why it is never secrecy on its own. The claim is decided for every one of the 16 × 16 = 256 four-bit pairs, using this wing’s own axiom-free lxor rather than Lean’s native Nat.xor, whose well-founded recursion is not kernel-only.
lessons.why: THE XOR CHECKSUM IS ITS OWN UNDOING, OVER ALL 256 PAIRS. Applying a key twice returns the message — (a XOR b) XOR b = a — which is why XOR is a checksum and a cipher at once, and why it is never secrecy on its own. The claim is decided for every one of the 16 × 16 = 256 four-bit pairs, using this wing’s own axiom-free lxor rather than Lean’s native Nat.xor, whose well-founded recursion is not kernel-only.
lessons.statement: ((List.range 16).all (fun a => (List.range 16).all (fun b => lxor (lxor a b) b == a))) ∧ (16 * 16 = 256)
